anti_overlap: Does not evaluate the API's standalone commercial viability, agent-builder market sizing, or open-core pricing — that is fd-api-business-viability's territory.
Does not evaluate FLUX licensing, privacy-gate correctness, or other legal/commercial prerequisites — that is fd-ip-privacy-compliance's territory.
Focuses on tier sequencing, activation economics, and the ambient-channel question, not on whether the API itself is a sellable product.
decision_lens: Ask what a paying subscriber actually experiences in session one, week one, and the first billing cycle — then check whether the plan as sequenced produces that experience, or produces the exact 'generic chat client the ablation says a system prompt reproduces' outcome the memo warns against, just relabeled as an intermediate tier.
focus: Whether the memo's recommended tier ordering (API, then profile, then mobile app last) actually serves pivot survival or instead defers the ambient channel and profile — the one thing the memo itself says makes Auraken more than a system prompt — past the point where a paid FLUX-reader consumer product could show day-one value.
name: fd-mobile-subscription-sequencing
persona: Apply the perspective of a consumer mobile-subscription product strategist with experience in activation and retention economics, habit-formation design, and day-1-through-day-90 value curves for paid apps — someone who has watched a subscription product lose its trial cohort while its real differentiator was still three quarters away on the roadmap.
review_areas: Test the memo's own stated logic against its own recommended order: §3 says the mobile app's "one load-bearing justification" is the ambient channel/slow-drift watcher (directive 4), yet §4-5's recommended sequencing builds that exact capability in Tier 3, last, after "weeks" of Tier 1 and "one to two months" of Tier 2 — check whether the memo ever reconciles building the thing it calls load-bearing dead last.

Examine the unresolved day-one problem: §3 names it explicitly ("a paid app that charges from day one is selling the ninety-day product on day one's evidence") but §4-5's recommendation doesn't resolve it for Tier 3 — it just moves Tier 3 later, so the same subscriber who signs up when the app finally ships still gets the thinking-domain-only, ablation-replicable experience on day one; verify whether "later" is actually different from "unsolved."

Identify day-one consumer-product requirements the memo never names for the eventual FLUX-reader subscriber: onboarding/first-run design, trial-to-paid conversion mechanics, paywall placement, an App Store listing that doesn't oversell what day-one delivers, and any retention hook besides the (Tier-3, not-yet-built) ambient channel.

Check for an asymmetric standard between options: §4 Option A's stated risk is "the profile that justifies the price does not exist" during a six-month build; Option B/Tier 3 has structurally the same gap (the ambient channel doesn't exist until Tier 3), just deferred and reframed as "pivot survival" — test whether the memo applies a harsher standard to the option it rejects (A) than to the one it recommends (B).

Test the "reference user" claim in §3: mk's own instance becoming "the reference user and dogfood environment" is asserted as a consequence of the audience-axis pivot, not designed — since every finding in §2 is derived from an n=1 instrument (per Option D's own framing), check whether the memo specifies how a cold-start non-mk FLUX reader's profile is expected to reach comparable value, or whether that transfer is simply assumed.

Verify the ablation argument in §3 is applied consistently: it's used to undercut the API/selector's differentiation claim, but the mobile app's stated differentiator (the ambient channel) is never run through the same 'would a frontier model/competitor reproduce this' test, and no §7 falsification test targets the ambient channel's actual retention value.

severity_examples.condition: §4-5 sequence Tier 3 (mobile app / ambient channel) after Tiers 1-2 ship and are marketed, with no interim design for what a paying subscriber experiences before Tier 3 lands.
severity_examples.scenario: The recommended sequencing (B/C) builds directive 4's ambient channel — the memo's own stated sole justification for a mobile app (§3) — in Tier 3, last, so any subscriber who pays during Tiers 1-2's public existence experiences exactly the 'chat client... the ablation says a system prompt reproduces' outcome the memo warns against, for months, under the same 'paid product sold on day-one evidence' failure mode Option A was marked risky for.

severity_examples.condition: No day-one activation/retention design is specified for Tier 2 or Tier 3's eventual consumer-facing product.
severity_examples.scenario: mk rules for B/C expecting the day-one problem named in §3 to be handled, but no onboarding, paywall-timing, or non-ambient retention design appears anywhere in the memo for the eventual FLUX-reader subscriber, so the day-one problem is named but not designed around at any tier.

severity_examples.condition: No plan or evidence for cold-start profile parity appears in §2-§5.
severity_examples.scenario: The 'reference user and dogfood environment' consequence (§3) is stated but undesigned — a non-mk cold-start user's profile has none of mk's accumulated context, and since every finding in §2 traces to an n=1 instrument, the memo gives mk no way to judge how much of the moat actually transfers to a stranger.

success_hints: Directly engages the task's framing — does API-first defer the ambient channel/profile — and locates the tension precisely in §3 through §5 rather than restating the memo's own risk language back at it.
Cites subscription-product norms (trial-to-paid windows, early-retention benchmarks) as an external check on the 'moat arrives around day ninety' claim rather than only asserting it's risky.

Distinguishes the mobile app's stated justification (ambient channel) from the API's stated justification (structured output) and evaluates each against its own evidence instead of treating 'mobile app' as one undifferentiated risk.
Names the asymmetry between how Option A's day-one gap is treated (a listed risk) and how Tier 3's identical gap is treated (an accepted consequence of sequencing) if it's there.
Proposes what a day-one FLUX-reader product actually needs (onboarding, paywall placement, a non-ambient retention hook) rather than only flagging the absence.
task_context: This is a pre-ruling stress review of a product-fork memo (`docs/2026-09-03-product-fork-memo.md`) proposing what Auraken should become if mk ships it as a paid mobile app plus an agent/model API endpoint — the memo lays out four options (A: mobile-first; B: API-first, recommended; C: open-core framing of B; D: stay n=1) and asks mk to rule on the audience axis. Stress the memo before mk rules on it: (1) is 'API first, mobile last' actually the pivot-surviving order, or does it defer the only thing (the ambient channel + profile) that makes Auraken more than a system prompt; (2) is a stateless soundpost API a real market for anyone, given the repo's own ablation says a frontier model improvises the lens equally well; (3) what does the memo miss that a paid consumer product for FLUX readers would need on day one; (4) are the FLUX-licensing and privacy-gate claims stated correctly and are there other legal/commercial prerequisites unnamed. Surface missed options and cheaper falsification tests. A wrong ruling here costs months of build on a sixth product shape.
